subject: Dermatology
question: A 41-year-old man develops itchy, polygonal, violaceous papules on the flexor aspect of his forearms. Some of these papules have coalesced to form plaques. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen xplanus: purple, pruritic, papular, polygonal rash on flexor surfaces. Wickham's striae over surface. Oral involvement common xsclerosus: itchy white spots typically seen on the vulva of elderly women

Lichen planus Lichen planus is a skin disorder of unknown aetiology, most probably being immune mediated Features xitchy, papular rash most common on the palms, soles, genitalia and flexor surfaces of arms xrash often polygonal in shape, 'white-lace' pattern on the surface (Wickham's striae) xKoebner phenomenon may be seen (new skin lesions appearing at the site of trauma) xoral involvement in around 50% of patients xnails: thinning of nail plate, longitudinal ridging

Lichenoid drug eruptions - causes: xgold xquinine xthiazides

Management xtopical steroids are the mainstay of treatment xextensive lichen planus may require oral steroids or immunosuppression

subject: Dermatology
question: A 30-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy mentions during an antenatal appointment that she has noticed an itchy rash around her umbilicus. This is her second pregnancy and she had no similar problems in her first pregnancy. Examination reveals blistering lesions in the peri-umbilical region and on her arms. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is not associated with blistering

Pemphigoid gestationis is the correct answer. Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is not associated with blistering Skin disorders associated with pregnancy

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy xpruritic condition associated with last trimester xlesions often first appear in abdominal striae xmanagement depends on severity: emollients, mild potency topical steroids and oral steroids may be used

Pemphigoid gestationis xpruritic blistering lesions xoften develop in peri-umbilical region, later spreading to the trunk, back, buttocks and arms xusually presents 2nd or 3rd trimester and is rarely seen in the first pregnancy xoral corticosteroids are usually required

subject: Dermatology
question: A 62-year-old female is referred to dermatology due to a lesion over her shin. It initially started as a small red papule which later became a deep, red, necrotic ulcer with a violaceous border. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a classic description of pyoderma gangrenosum Shin lesions

The differential diagnosis of shin lesions includes the following conditions: xerythema nodosum xpretibial myxoedema xpyoderma gangrenosum xnecrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum

Below are the characteristic features: Erythema nodosum xsymmetrical, erythematous, tender, nodules which heal without scarring xmost common causes are streptococcal infections, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease and drugs (penicillins, sulphonamides, oral contraceptive pill)

Pretibial myxoedema xsymmetrical, erythematous lesions seen in Graves' disease xshiny, orange peel skin

Pyoderma gangrenosum xinitially small red papule xlater deep, red, necrotic ulcers with a violaceous border xidiopathic in 50%, may also be seen in inflammatory bowel disease, connective tissue disorders and myeloproliferative disorders

Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum xshiny, painless areas of yellow/red skin typically on the shin of diabetics xoften associated with telangiectasia

subject: Dermatology
question: A 39-year-old female has a pigmented mole removed from her leg which histology shows to be a malignant melanoma. What is the single most important prognostic marker?

options.A: Number of episodes of sunburn before the age of 18 years

explanation:
Melanoma: the invasion depth of the tumour is the single most important prognostic factor

Malignant melanoma: prognostic factors The invasion depth of a tumour (Breslow depth) is the single most important factor in determining prognosis of patients with malignant melanoma Breslow Thickness Approximate 5 year survival < 1 mm 95-100% 1 - 2 mm 80-96% 2.1 - 4 mm 60-75% > 4 mm 50%

subject: Dermatology
question: A 62-year-old female is referred due to a long-standing ulcer above the right medial malleolus. Ankle-brachial pressure index readings are as follows: Right 0.95 Left 0.95 To date it has been managed by the District Nurse with standard dressings. What is the most appropriate management to maximize the likelihood of the ulcer healing?
explanation:
Management of venous ulceration - compression bandaging

The ankle-brachial pressure index readings indicate a reasonable arterial supply and suggest the ulcers are venous in nature. Venous ulceration Venous ulceration is typically seen above the medial malleolus

Investigations xankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) is important in non-healing ulcers to assess for poor arterial flow which could impair healing xa 'normal' ABPI may be regarded as between 0.9 - 1.2. Values below 0.9 indicate arterial disease. Interestingly, values above 1.3 may also indicate arterial disease, in the form of false-negative results secondary to arterial calcification (e.g. In diabetics)

Management xcompression bandaging, usually four layer (only treatment shown to be of real benefit) xoral pentoxifylline, a peripheral vasodilator, improves healing rate xsmall evidence base supporting use of flavinoids

xlittle evidence to suggest benefit from hydrocolloid dressings, topical growth factors, ultrasound therapy and intermittent pneumatic compression

subject: Dermatology
question: A 40-year-old man complains of widespread pruritus for the past two weeks. The itching is particularly bad at night. He has no history of note and works in the local car factory. On examination he has noted to have a number of linear erythematous lesions in between his fingers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Scabies Scabies is caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei and is spread by prolonged skin contact. It typically affects children and young adults.

The scabies mite burrows into the skin, laying its eggs in the stratum corneum. The intense pruritus associatedwith scabies is due to a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction to mites/eggs which occurs about 30 days after the initial infection.

Features xwidespread pruritus xlinear burrows on the side of fingers, interdigital webs and flexor aspects of the wrist xin infants the face and scalp may also be affected xsecondary features are seen due to scratching: excoriation, infection

Management xpermethrin 5% is first-line xmalathion 0.5% is second-line xgive appropriate guidance on use (see below) xpruritus persists for up to 4-6 weeks post eradication

Patient guidance on treatment (from Clinical Knowledge Summaries) xavoid close physical contact with others until treatment is complete xall household and close physical contacts should be treated at the same time, even if asymptomatic xlaunder, iron or tumble dry clothing, bedding, towels, etc., on the first day of treatment to kill off mites.

The BNF advises to apply the insecticide to all areas, including the face and scalp, contrary to the manufacturer's recommendation. Patients should be given the following instructions: xapply the insecticide cream or liquid to cool, dry skin xpay close attention to areas between fingers and toes, under nails, armpit area, creases of the skin such as at the wrist and elbow xallow to dry and leave on the skin for 8-12 hours for permethrin, or for 24 hours for malathion, before washing off xreapply if insecticide is removed during the treatment period, e.g. If wash hands, change nappy, etc xrepeat treatment 7 days later

subject: Dermatology
question: A 22-year-old woman presents due to hypopigmented skin lesions on her chest and back. She has recently returned from the south of France and has tanned skin. On examination the lesions are slightly scaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pityriasis versicolor Pityriasis versicolor, also called tinea versicolor, is a superficial cutaneous fungal infection caused by Malassezia furfur (formerly termed Pityrosporum ovale)

Features xmost commonly affects trunk xpatches may be hypopigmented, pink or brown (hence versicolor) xscale is common xmild pruritus

Predisposing factors xoccurs in healthy individuals ximmunosuppression xmalnutrition xCushing's

Management xtopical antifungal e.g. terbinafine or selenium sulphide xif extensive disease or failure to respond to topical treatment then consider oral itraconazole

subject: Dermatology
question: A 67-year-old man with a history of Parkinson's disease presents due to the development of an itchy, red rash on his neck, behind his ears and around the nasolabial folds. He had a similar flare up last winter but did not seek medical attention. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Seborrhoeic dermatitis is more common in patients with Parkinson's disease Seborrhoeic dermatitis in adults Seborrhoeic dermatitis in adults is a chronic dermatitis thought to be caused by an inflammatory reaction related to a proliferation of a normal skin inhabitant, a fungus called Malassezia furfur (formerly known as Pityrosporum ovale). It is common, affecting around 2% of the general population

Features xeczematous lesions on the sebum-rich areas: scalp (may cause dandruff), periorbital, auricular and nasolabial folds xotitis externa and blepharitis may develop

Associated conditions include xHIV xParkinson's disease

Scalp disease management xover the counter preparations containing zinc pyrithione ('Head & Shoulders') and tar ('Neutrogena T/Gel') are first-line xthe preferred second-line agent is ketoconazole xselenium sulphide and topical corticosteroid may also be useful

Face and body management xtopical antifungals: e.g. Ketoconazole xtopical steroids: best used for short periods xdifficult to treat - recurrences are common

subject: Dermatology
question: A 43-year-old man comes for review. A few months ago he developed redness around his nose and cheeks. This is worse after drinking alcohol. He is concerned as one of his work colleagues asked him if he had a drink problem despite him drinking 14 units per week. On examination he has erythema as described above with some pustules on the nose and telangiectasia on the cheeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a typical history of acne rosacea Acne rosacea Acne rosacea is a chronic skin disease of unknown aetiology

Features xtypically affects nose, cheeks and forehead xflushing is often first symptom xtelangiectasia are common xlater develops into persistent erythema with papules and pustules xrhinophyma xocular involvement: blepharitis

Management xtopical metronidazole may be used for mild symptoms (i.e. Limited number of papules and pustules, no plaques) xmore severe disease is treated with systemic antibiotics e.g. Oxytetracycline xrecommend daily application of a high-factor sunscreen xcamouflage creams may help conceal redness xlaser therapy may be appropriate for patients with prominent telangiectasia

subject: Dermatology
question: A 19-year-old student presents with a three day history of a 1 cm golden, crusted lesion on the border of her lower lip. What is the most suitable management?
explanation:
Impetigo - topical fusidic acid --> oral flucloxacillin / topical retapamulin

This history is typical of impetigo. As the lesion is small and localised topical fusidic acid is recommended Impetigo: management

Limited, localised disease xtopical fusidic acid is first-line xtopical retapamulin is used second-line if fusidic acid has been ineffective or is not tolerated xMRSA is not susceptible to either fusidic acid or retapamulin. Topical mupirocin (Bactroban) should therefore be used in this situation

Extensive disease xoral flucloxacillin xoral erythromycin if penicillin allergic

subject: Dermatology
question: A 74-year-old lady with a history of hypothyroidism presents in January with a rash down the right side of her body. On examination an erythematous rash with patches of hyperpigmentation and telangiectasia is found. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a classic presentation of erythema ab igne. Despite the name, pretibial myxoedema is associated with hyperthyroidism rather than hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism can make patients feel cold and hence more likely to sit next a heater / fire. Erythema ab igne Erythema ab igne is a skin disorder caused by over exposure to infrared radiation. Characteristic features include reticulated, erythematous patches with hyperpigmentation and telangiectasia. A typical history would be an elderly women who always sits next to an open fire

If the cause is not treated then patients may go on to develop squamous cell skin cancer

subject: Dermatology
question: A 28-year-old man presents with multiple protuberant lesions around the anus which have been present for about 6 weeks. He reports it is painful when he passes a stool although there is no change in bowel habit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ambiguous questions such as this are common in the MRCP. Whilst a case could be made for any of the answers the most likely cause from the above list, in a 28-year-old male, is genital warts Genital warts

Genital warts (also known as condylomata accuminata) are a common cause of attendance at genitourinary clinics. They are caused by the many varieties of the human papilloma virus HPV, especially types 6 & 11. It is now well established that HPV (primarily types 16,18 & 33) predisposes to cervical cancer.

Features xsmall (2 - 5 mm) fleshy protuberances which are slightly pigmented xmay bleed or itch

Management xtopical podophyllum or cryotherapy are commonly used as first-line treatments depending on the location and type of lesion. Multiple, non-keratinised warts are generally best treated with topical agents whereas solitary, keratinised warts respond better to cryotherapy ximiquimod is a topical cream which is generally used second line xgenital warts are often resistant to treatment and recurrence is common although the majority of anogenital infections with HPV clear without intervention within 1-2 years

subject: Dermatology
question: A 25-year-old man presents with a widespread rash over his body. The torso and limbs are covered with multiple erythematous lesions less than 1 cm in diameter which in parts are covered by a fine scale. You note that two weeks earlier he was seen with to a sore throat when it was noted that he had exudative tonsillitis. Other than a history of asthma he is normally fit and well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Psoriasis: guttate Guttate psoriasis is more common in children and adolescents. It may be precipitated by a streptococcal infection 2-4 weeks prior to the lesions appearing

Features xtear drop papules on the trunk and limbs

Management xmost cases resolve spontaneously within 2-3 months xthere is no firm evidence to support the use of antibiotics to eradicate streptococcal infection xtopical agents as per psoriasis xUVB phototherapy xtonsillectomy may be necessary with recurrent episodes

subject: Dermatology
question: A 25-year-old man presents with a pruritic skin rash. This has been present for the past few weeks and has responded poorly to an emollient cream. The pruritus is described as 'intense' and has resulted in him having trouble sleeping. On inspecting the skin you notice a combination of papules and vesicles on his buttocks and the extensor aspect of the knees and elbows. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Dermatitis herpetiformis Dermatitis herpetiformis is an autoimmune blistering skin disorder associated with coeliac disease. It is caused by deposition of IgA in the dermis.

Features xitchy, vesicular skin lesions on the extensor surfaces (e.g. elbows, knees buttocks)

Diagnosis xskin biopsy: direct immunofluorescence shows deposition of IgA in a granular pattern in the upper dermis

Management xgluten-free diet xdapsone

subject: Dermatology
question: A 54-year-old man is referred to the dermatology outpatient department due to a facial rash which has persisted for the past 12 months. On examination there is a symmetrical rash consisting of extensive pustules and papules which affects his nose, cheeks and forehead. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Acne rosacea treatment: xmild/moderate: topical metronidazole xsevere/resistant: oral tetracycline

As there is extensive involvement oral oxytetracycline should probably be used rather than topical metronidazole Acne rosacea

Acne rosacea is a chronic skin disease of unknown aetiology

Features xtypically affects nose, cheeks and forehead xflushing is often first symptom xtelangiectasia are common xlater develops into persistent erythema with papules and pustules xrhinophyma xocular involvement: blepharitis

Management xtopical metronidazole may be used for mild symptoms (i.e. Limited number of papules and pustules, no plaques) xmore severe disease is treated with systemic antibiotics e.g. Oxytetracycline xrecommend daily application of a high-factor sunscreen xcamouflage creams may help conceal redness xlaser therapy may be appropriate for patients with prominent telangiectasia

subject: Dermatology
question: A 23-year-old man presents with a three day history of general malaise and low-grade temperature. Yesterday he developed extensive painful ulceration of his mouth and gums. On examination his temperature is 37.4ºC, pulse 84 / min and there is submandibular lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This man has gingivostomatitis, a characteristic feature of primary herpes simplex virus infection Herpes simplex virus There are two strains of the herpes simplex virus (HSV) in humans: HSV-1 and HSV-2. Whilst it was previously thought HSV-1 accounted for oral lesions (cold sores) and HSV-2 for genital herpes it is now known there is considerable overlap

Features xprimary infection: may present with a severe gingivostomatitis xcold sores xpainful genital ulceration

Management xgingivostomatitis: oral aciclovir, chlorhexidine mouthwash xcold sores: topical aciclovir although the evidence base for this is modest xgenital herpes: oral aciclovir. Some patients with frequent exacerbations may benefit from longer term aciclovir

subject: Dermatology
question: Which one of the following conditions is most strongly associated with erythema multiforme?
explanation:
This is difficult as both herpes simplex and streptococcal infections are known causes of erythema multiforme (EM). However, studies suggest that HSV is the trigger in over 50% of cases. Streptococcal infections and sarcoidosis are more strongly associated with erythema nodosum Erythema multiforme

Features xtarget lesions xinitially seen on the back of the hands / feet before spreading to the torso xupper limbs are more commonly affected than the lower limbs xpruritus is occasionally seen and is usually mild If symptoms are severe and involve blistering and mucosal involvement the term Stevens-Johnson syndrome is used.

Causes xviruses: herpes simplex virus (the most common cause), Orf* xidiopathic xbacteria: Mycoplasma, Streptococcus

xdrugs: penicillin, sulphonamides, carbamazepine, allopurinol, NSAIDs, oral contraceptive pill, nevirapine xconnective tissue disease e.g. Systemic lupus erythematosus xsarcoidosis xmalignancy *Orf is a skin disease of sheep and goats caused by a parapox virus

subject: Dermatology
question: Which of the following conditions is most associated with onycholysis?
explanation:
Raynaud's disease causes onycholysis, as can any cause of impaired circulation Onycholysis Onycholysis describes the separation of the nail plate from the nail bed

Causes xidiopathic xtrauma e.g. Excessive manicuring xinfection: especially fungal xskin disease: psoriasis, dermatitis ximpaired peripheral circulation e.g. Raynaud's xsystemic disease: hyper- and hypothyroidism

subject: Dermatology
question: A 34-year-old man presents for the removal of a mole. Where on the body are keloid scars most likely to form?
explanation:
Keloid scars are most common on the sternum

Keloid scars Keloid scars are tumour-like lesions that arise from the connective tissue of a scar and extend beyond the dimensions of the original wound

Predisposing factors xethnicity: more common in people with dark skin xoccur more commonly in young adults, rare in the elderly xcommon sites (in order of decreasing frequency): sternum, shoulder, neck, face, extensor surface of limbs, trunk

Keloid scars are less likely if incisions are made along relaxed skin tension lines*

Treatment xearly keloids may be treated with intra-lesional steroids e.g. triamcinolone

xexcision is sometimes required *Langer lines were historically used to determine the optimal incision line. They were based on procedures done on cadavers but have been shown to produce worse cosmetic results than when following skin tension lines

subject: Dermatology
question: A 45-year-old woman presents for review. She has noticed a number of patches of 'pale skin' on her hands over the past few weeks. The patient has tried using an emollient and topical hydrocortisone with no result. On examination you note a number of hypopigmented patches on the dorsum of both hands. Her past medical history includes thyrotoxicosis for which she takes carbimazole and thyroxine. What is the most likely causes of her symptoms?
explanation:
Vitiligo is more common in patients with known autoimmune conditions such as thyrotoxicosis. There is nothing else in the history to suggest Addison disease. Vitiligo Vitiligo is an autoimmune condition which results in the loss of melanocytes and consequent depigmentation of the skin. It is thought to affect around 1% of the population and symptoms typically develop by the age of 20-30 years.

Features xwell demarcated patches of depigmented skin xthe peripheries tend to be most affected xtrauma may precipitate new lesions (Koebner phenomenon)

Associated conditions xtype 1 diabetes mellitus xAddison's disease xautoimmune thyroid disorders xpernicious anaemia xalopecia areata

Management xsun block for affected areas of skin xcamouflage make-up xtopical corticosteroids may reverse the changes if applied early xthere may also be a role for topical tacrolimus and phototherapy, although caution needs to be exercised with light-skinned patients

subject: Dermatology
question: Which one of the following complications is most associated with psoralen + ultraviolet A light (PUVA) therapy?
explanation:
The most significant complication of PUVA therapy for psoriasis is squamous cell skin cancer. Psoriasis: management SIGN released guidelines in 2010 on the management of psoriasis and psoriatic arthropathy. Please see the link for more details.

Chronic plaque psoriasis xregular emollients may help to reduce scale loss and reduce pruritus xfor acute control SIGN recommend: 'Short term intermittent use of a potent topical corticosteroid or a combined potent corticosteroid plus calcipotriol ointment is recommended to gain rapid improvement in plaque psoriasis.' x'For long term topical treatment of plaque psoriasis a vitamin D analogue (e.g. Calcipotriol) is recommended.' x'If a vitamin D analogue is ineffective or not tolerated then consider coal tar (solution, cream or lotion), tazarotene gel, or short contact dithranol (30 minute exposure in patients with a small number of relatively large plaques of psoriasis).

Steroids in psoriasis xtopical steroids are commonly used in flexural psoriasis and there is also a role for mild steroids in facial psoriasis. If steroids are ineffective for these conditions vitamin D analogues or tacrolimus ointment should be used second line xSIGN caution against the long term use of potent or very potent topical steroids due to the risk of sideeffects

Scalp psoriasis xfor short term control SIGN recommend either the use of potent topical corticosteroids or a combination of a potent corticosteroid and a vitamin D analogue x'For patients with thick scaling of the scalp, initial treatment with overnight application of salicylic acid, tar preparations, or oil preparations (eg olive oil, coconut oil) to remove thick scale is recommended.

Secondary care management

Phototherapy xnarrow band ultraviolet B light (311-313nm) is now the treatment of choice xphotochemotherapy is also used - psoralen + ultraviolet A light (PUVA) xadverse effects: skin ageing, squamous cell cancer (not melanoma)

Systemic therapy xmethotrexate: useful if associated joint disease xciclosporin xsystemic retinoids xbiological agents: infliximab, etanercept and adalimumab xustekinumab (IL-12 and IL-23 blocker) is showing promise in early trials

Mechanism of action of commonly used drugs: xcoal tar: probably inhibit DNA synthesis xcalcipotriol: vitamin D analogue which reduces epidermal proliferation and restores a normal horny layer xdithranol: inhibits DNA synthesis, wash off after 30 mins, SE: burning, staining

subject: Dermatology
question: A 38-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis and epilepsy presents with generalised increased hair growth over her trunk and arms. Which one of the following drugs is associated with hypertrichosis?
explanation:
Phenytoin is associated with hirsutism rather than hypertrichosis Hirsutism and hypertrichosis /hirsutism is often used to describe androgen-dependent hair growth in women, with hypertrichosis being used for androgen-independent hair growth

Polycystic ovarian syndrome is the most common causes of hirsutism. Other causes include: xCushing's syndrome xcongenital adrenal hyperplasia xandrogen therapy xobesity: due to peripheral conversion oestrogens to androgens xadrenal tumour xandrogen secreting ovarian tumour xdrugs: phenytoin

Assessment of hirsutism xFerriman-Gallwey scoring system: 9 body areas are assigned a score of 0 - 4, a score > 15 is considered to indicate moderate or severe hirsutism

Management of hirsutism xadvise weight loss if overweight xcosmetic techniques such as waxing/bleaching - not available on the NHS xconsider using combined oral contraceptive pills such as co-cyprindiol (Dianette) or ethinylestradiol and drospirenone (Yasmin). Co-cyprindiol should not be used long-term due to the increased risk of venous thromboembolism xfacial hirsutism: topical eflornithine - contraindicated in pregnancy and breast-feeding

Causes of hypertrichosis xdrugs: minoxidil, ciclosporin, diazoxide xcongenital hypertrichosis lanuginosa, congenital hypertrichosis terminalis xporphyria cutanea tarda xanorexia nervosa

question: A 64-year-old patient is referred to dermatology outpatients due to a rash. A diagnosis necrolytic migratory erythema is made. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Skin disorders associated with malignancy

subject: Dermatology
question: A 31-year-old woman develops with painful, purple lesions on her shins. Which one of the following medications is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum

Overview xinflammation of subcutaneous fat xtypically causes tender, erythematous, nodular lesions xusually occurs over shins, may also occur elsewhere (e.g. forearms, thighs) xusually resolves within 6 weeks xlesions heal without scarring

Causes xinfection: streptococci, TB, brucellosis xsystemic disease: sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, Behcet's xmalignancy/lymphoma xdrugs: penicillins, sulphonamides, combined oral contraceptive pill xpregnancy

subject: Dermatology
question: Which one of the following conditions is least likely to be associated with pyoderma gangrenosum?
explanation:
Syphilis is not commonly associated with pyoderma gangrenosum Pyoderma gangrenosum

Features xtypically on the lower limbs xinitially small red papule

xlater deep, red, necrotic ulcers with a violaceous border xmay be accompanied systemic symptoms e.g. Fever, myalgia

Causes* xidiopathic in 50% xinflammatory bowel disease: ulcerative colitis, Crohn's xrheumatoid arthritis, SLE xmyeloproliferative disorders xlymphoma, myeloid leukaemias xmonoclonal gammopathy (IgA) xprimary biliary cirrhosis

Management xthe potential for rapid progression is high in most patients and most doctors advocate oral steroids as first-line treatment xother immunosuppressive therapy, for example ciclosporin and infliximab, have a role in difficult cases *note whilst pyoderma gangrenosum can occur in diabetes mellitus it is rare and is generally not included in a differential of potential causes

subject: Dermatology
question: A 36-year-old woman is reviewed. She presented 4 weeks ago with itchy dry skin on her arms and was diagnosed as having atopic eczema. She was prescribed hydrocortisone 1% cream with an emollient. Unfortunately there has been no improvement in her symptoms. What is the next step in management, alongside continued regular use of an emollient?
explanation:
Topical steroids xmoderate: Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% xpotent: Betamethasone valerate 0.1% xvery potent: Clobetasol propionate 0.05%

Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% is a moderately potent topical steroid and would be the most suitable next step in management. It is important to note the potency difference between two very similar sounding steroids - Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% (moderate) and Clobetasol propionate 0.05% (very potent) Eczema: topical steroids Use weakest steroid cream which controls patients symptoms The table below shows topical steroids by potency Mild Moderate Potent Very potent

Hydrocortisone 0.5- 2.5%

Betamethasone valerate 0.025% (Betnovate RD) Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% (Eumovate)

Fluticasone propionate 0.05% (Cutivate) Betamethasone valerate 0.1% (Betnovate)

Clobetasol propionate 0.05% (Dermovate)

Finger tip rule x1 finger tip unit (FTU) = 0.5 g, sufficient to treat a skin area about twice that of the flat of an adult hand

Topical steroid doses for eczema in adults Area of skin Fingertip units per dose Hand and fingers (front and back) 1.0 A foot (all over) 2.0 Front of chest and abdomen 7.0 Back and buttocks 7.0 Face and neck 2.5 An entire arm and hand 4.0 An entire leg and foot 8.0

The BNF makes recommendation on the quantity of topical steroids that should be prescribed for an adult for a single daily application for 2 weeks: Area Amount Face and neck 15 to 30 g Both hands 15 t Scalp 15 to 30 g Both arms 30 to 60 g Both legs 100 g Trunk 100 g Groin and genitalia 15 to 30 g

subject: Dermatology
question: A 54-year-old man presents with a brown velvety rash on the back of his neck around his axilla. A clinical diagnosis of acanthosis nigricans is made. Which one of the following conditions is most associated with this kind of rash?
explanation:
Acanthosis nigricans Describes symmetrical, brown, velvety plaques that are often found on the neck, axilla and groin

Causes xgastrointestinal cancer xinsulin-resistant diabetes mellitus xobesity xpolycystic ovarian syndrome xacromegaly xCushing's disease xhypothyroidism xfamilial xPrader-Willi syndrome xdrugs: oral contraceptive pill, nicotinic acid

subject: Dermatology
question: A 67-year-old man who is a retired builder presents following the development of a number of red, scaly lesions on his left temple. These were initially small and flat but are now erythematous and rough to touch. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Actinic keratoses Actinic, or solar, keratoses (AK) is a common premalignant skin lesion that develops as a consequence of chronic sun exposure

Features xsmall, crusty or scaly, lesions xmay be pink, red, brown or the same colour as the skin xtypically on sun-exposed areas e.g. temples of head xmultiple lesions may be present

Management options include xprevention of further risk: e.g. sun avoidance, sun cream xfluorouracil cream: typically a 2 to 3 week course. The skin will become red and inflamed - sometimes topical hydrocortisone is given following fluorouracil to help settle the inflammation xtopical diclofenac: may be used for mild AKs. Moderate efficacy but much fewer side-effects xtopical imiquimod: trials have shown good efficacy xcryotherapy xcurettage and cautery

question: A 85-year-old lady presents to dermatology clinic complaining of itchy white plaques affecting her vulva. There is no history of vaginal discharge or bleeding. A similar plaque is also seen on her inner thigh. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen xplanus: purple, pruritic, papular, polygonal rash on flexor surfaces. Wickham's striae over surface. Oral involvement common xsclerosus: itchy white spots typically seen on the vulva of elderly women

The correct answer is lichen sclerosus. Candida may cause pruritus and white plaques but lesions would not also be seen on her inner thigh Lichen sclerosus Lichen sclerosus was previously termed lichen sclerosus et atrophicus. It is an inflammatory condition which usually affects the genitalia and is more common in elderly females. Lichen sclerosus leads to atrophy of the epidermis with white plaques forming

Features xitch is prominent

A biopsy is often performed to exclude other diagnoses

Management xtopical steroids and emollients xincreased risk of vulval cancer

subject: Dermatology
question: A 26-year-old newly qualified nurse presents as she has developed a bilateral erythematous rash on both hands. She has recently emigrated from the Philippines and has no past medical history of note. A diagnosis of contact dermatitis is suspected. What is the most suitable to test to identify the underlying cause?
explanation:
The skin patch test is useful in this situation as it may also identify for irritants, not just allergens Allergy tests Skin prick test Most commonly used test as easy to perform and inexpensive. Drops of diluted allergen are placed on the skin after which the skin is pierced using a needle. A large number of allergens can be tested in one session. Normally includes a histamine (positive) and sterile water (negative) control. A wheal will typically develop if a patient has an allergy. Can be interpreted after 15 minutes Useful for food allergies and also pollen Radioallergosorbent test (RAST)

Determines the amount of IgE that reacts specifically with suspected or known allergens, for example IgE to egg protein. Results are given in grades from 0 (negative) to 6 (strongly positive)

Useful for food allergies, inhaled allergens (e.g. Pollen) and wasp/bee venom

Blood tests may be used when skin prick tests are not suitable, for example if there is extensive eczema or if the patient is taking antihistamines

Skin patch testing Useful for contact dermatitis. Around 30-40 allergens are placed on the back. Irritants may also be tested for. The patches are removed 48 hours later with the results being read by a dermatologist after a further 48 hours

subject: Dermatology
question: A 43-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a rash and feeling generally unwell. He is known to have epilepsy and his medication was recently changed to phenytoin three weeks ago. Around one week ago he started to develop mouth ulcers associated with malaise and a cough. Two days ago he started to develop a widespread red rash which has now coalesced to form large fluid-filled blisters, covering around 30% of his body area. The lesions separate when slight pressure is applied. On examination his temperature is 38.3ºC and pulse 126 / min. Blood results show: Na+ 144 mmol/l K+ 4.2 mmol/l Bicarbonate 19 mmol/l Urea 13.4 mmol/l Creatinine 121 μmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Toxic epidermal necrolysis Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is a potentially life-threatening skin disorder that is most commonly seen secondary to a drug reaction. In this condition the skin develops a scalded appearance over an extensive area. Some authors consider TEN to be the severe end of a spectrum of skin disorders which includes erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome

Features xsystemically unwell e.g. pyrexia, tachycardic xpositive Nikolsky's sign: the epidermis separates with mild lateral pressure

Drugs known to induce TEN xphenytoin xsulphonamides xallopurinol xpenicillins xcarbamazepine xNSAIDs

Management xstop precipitating factor xsupportive care, often in intensive care unit xintravenous immunoglobulin has been shown to be effective and is now commonly used first-line xother treatment options include: immunosuppressive agents (ciclosporin and cyclophosphamide), plasmapheresis

subject: Dermatology
question: A 34-year-old man presents to dermatology clinic with an itchy rash on his palms. He has also noticed the rash around the site of a recent scar on his forearm. Examination reveals papules with a white-lace pattern on the surface. Some isolated white streaks are also noted on the mucous membranes of the mouth. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen xplanus: purple, pruritic, papular, polygonal rash on flexor surfaces. Wickham's striae over surface. Oral involvement common xsclerosus: itchy white spots typically seen on the vulva of elderly women

This is a typical history of lichen planus. Lichen planus Lichen planus is a skin disorder of unknown aetiology, most probably being immune mediated

Features xitchy, papular rash most common on the palms, soles, genitalia and flexor surfaces of arms xrash often polygonal in shape, 'white-lace' pattern on the surface (Wickham's striae) xKoebner phenomenon may be seen (new skin lesions appearing at the site of trauma) xoral involvement in around 50% of patients xnails: thinning of nail plate, longitudinal ridging

Lichenoid drug eruptions - causes: xgold xquinine xthiazides

Management xtopical steroids are the mainstay of treatment xextensive lichen planus may require oral steroids or immunosuppression

question: A 55-year-old female is referred to dermatology due to a lesions over both shins. On examination symmetrical erythematous lesions are found with an orange peel texture. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Shin lesions The differential diagnosis of shin lesions includes the following conditions: xerythema nodosum xpretibial myxoedema xpyoderma gangrenosum xnecrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum

Below are the characteristic features:

Pretibial myxoedema xsymmetrical, erythematous lesions seen in Graves' disease xshiny, orange peel skin

explanation:

question: Which of the following skin disorders is least associated with tuberculosis?
explanation:

Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous TB seen in the Indian subcontinent. It generally occurs on the face and is common around the nose and mouth. The initial lesion is an erythematous flat plaque which gradually becomes elevated and may ulcerate later

subject: Dermatology
question: Which one of the following statements regarding acne vulgaris is incorrect?

options.A: Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation results in obstruction of the
options.B: Acne vulgaris affects at least 80% of teenagers
options.C: Propionibacterium acnes is an anaerobic bacterium
options.D: Typical lesions include comedones and pustules
options.E: Beyond the age of 25 years acne vulgaris is more common in males

explanation:
Acne is actually more common in females after the age of 25 years Acne vulgaris Acne vulgaris is a common skin disorder which usually occurs in adolescence. It typically affects the face, neck and upper trunk and is characterised by the obstruction of the pilosebaceous follicle with keratin plugs which results in comedones, inflammation and pustules.

Epidemiology xaffects around 80-90% of teenagers, 60% of whom seek medical advice xacne may also persist beyond adolescence, with 10-15% of females and 5% of males over 25 years old being affected

Pathophysiology is multifactorial xfollicular epidermal hyperproliferation resulting in the formation of a keratin plug. This in turn causes obstruction of the pilosebaceous follicle. Activity of sebaceous glands may be controlled by androgen, although levels are often normal in patients with acne xcolonisation by the anaerobic bacterium Propionibacterium acnes xinflammation

question: A 23-year-old man presents with an itchy skin condition. Which one of the following is not part of the UK Working Party Diagnostic Criteria for atopic eczema?
explanation:
Whilst response to topical steroids provides useful clinical information it is not part of the diagnostic criteria. A wide variety of skin conditions can improve with topical steroid therapy. Eczema: diagnosis UK Working Party Diagnostic Criteria for Atopic Eczema

An itchy skin condition in the last 12 months Plus three or more of xonset below age 2 years* xhistory of flexural involvement** xhistory of generally dry skin xpersonal history of other atopic disease*** xvisible flexural dermatitis

explanation:
Acne rosacea Acne rosacea is a chronic skin disease of unknown aetiology

Features xtypically affects nose, cheeks and forehead xflushing is often first symptom xtelangiectasia are common xlater develops into persistent erythema with papules and pustules xrhinophyma xocular involvement: blepharitis

subject: Dermatology
question: A 26-year-old man who is HIV positive is noted to have developed seborrhoeic dermatitis. Which of the following two complications are most associated with this condition?
explanation:
Alopecia is not commonly seen in seborrhoeic dermatitis, but may develop if a severe secondary infection develops Seborrhoeic dermatitis in adults Seborrhoeic dermatitis in adults is a chronic dermatitis thought to be caused by an inflammatory reaction related to a proliferation of a normal skin inhabitant, a fungus called Malassezia furfur (formerly known as Pityrosporum ovale). It is common, affecting around 2% of the general population

Features xeczematous lesions on the sebum-rich areas: scalp (may cause dandruff), periorbital, auricular and nasolabial folds xotitis externa and blepharitis may develop

Associated conditions include xHIV xParkinson's disease

Scalp disease management xover the counter preparations containing zinc pyrithione ('Head & Shoulders') and tar ('Neutrogena T/Gel') are first-line xthe preferred second-line agent is ketoconazole xselenium sulphide and topical corticosteroid may also be useful

Face and body management xtopical antifungals: e.g. Ketoconazole xtopical steroids: best used for short periods xdifficult to treat - recurrences are common

question: A 26-year-old male presents with a rash. Examination reveals erythematous oval lesions on his back and upper arms which have a slight scale just inside the edge. They vary in size from 1 to 5 cm in diameter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The skin lesions seen in pityriasis rosea are generally larger than those found in guttate psoriasis and scaling is typically confined to just inside the edges Pityriasis rosea

Overview xcause unknown, herpes hominis virus 7 (HHV-7) a possibility xtends to affect young adults

Features xherald patch (usually on trunk) xfollowed by erythematous, oval, scaly patches which follow a characteristic distribution with the longitudinal diameters of the oval lesions running parallel to the line of Langer. This may produce a 'firtree' appearance

subject: Dermatology
question: Which of the following statements regarding psoriasis is incorrect?

options.B: Psoriatic arthropathy may occur prior to the development of skin lesions
options.C: Mediated by type 2 helper T cells
options.D: Abnormal T cell activity stimulates keratinocyte proliferation
options.E: Nail signs include pitting and onycholysis

explanation:
Psoriasis is mediated by type 1 helper T cells which are involved in the cell mediated response, rather than type 2 helper T cells Psoriasis Psoriasis is a common and chronic skin disorder. It generally presents with red, scaly patches on the skin although it is now recognised that patients with psoriasis are at increased risk of arthritis and cardiovascular disease.

Pathophysiology xmultifactorial and not yet fully understood xgenetic: associated HLA-B13, -B17, and -Cw6. Strong concordance (70%) in identical twins ximmunological: abnormal T cell activity stimulates keratinocyte proliferation. There is increasing evidence this may be mediated by a novel group of T helper cells producing IL-17, designated Th17.

These cells seem to be a third T-effector cell subset in addition to Th1 and Th2 xenvironmental: it is recognised that psoriasis may be worsened (e.g. Skin trauma, stress), triggered (e.g. Streptococcal infection) or improved (e.g. Sunlight) by environmental factors

Recognised subtypes of psoriasis xplaque psoriasis: the most common sub-type resulting in the typical well demarcated red, scaly patches affecting the extensor surfaces, sacrum and scalp xflexural psoriasis: in contrast to plaque psoriasis the skin is smooth xguttate psoriasis: transient psoriatic rash frequently triggered by a streptococcal infection. Multiple red, teardrop lesions appear on the body xpustular psoriasis: commonly occurs on the palms and soles

Other features xnail signs: pitting, onycholysis xarthritis

Complications xpsoriatic arthropathy (around 10%) xincreased incidence of metabolic syndrome xincreased incidence of cardiovascular disease xpsychological distress

subject: Dermatology
question: A 24-year-old woman presents due to a rash on her neck and forehead. She returned from a holiday in Cyprus 1 week ago and had her hair dyed 2 days ago. On examination there is a weepy, vesicular rash around her hairline although the scalp itself is not badly affected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Contact dermatitis There are two main types of contact dermatitis xirritant contact dermatitis: common - non-allergic reaction due to weak acids or alkalis (e.g. detergents). Often seen on the hands. Erythema is typical, crusting and vesicles are rare xallergic contact dermatitis: type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Uncommon - often seen on the head following hair dyes. Presents as an acute weeping eczema which predominately affects the margins of the hairline rather than the hairy scalp itself. Topical treatment with a potent steroid is indicated

Cement is a frequent cause of contact dermatitis. The alkaline nature of cement may cause an irritant contact dermatitis whilst the dichromates in cement also can cause an allergic contact dermatitis

subject: Dermatology
question: Which of the following conditions is least likely to exhibit the Koebner phenomenon?
explanation: Lupus vulgaris is not associated with the Koebner phenomenon Koebner phenomenon The Koebner phenomenon describes skin lesions which appear at the site of injury. It is seen in: xpsoriasis xvitiligo xwarts xlichen planus xlichen sclerosus xmolluscum contagiosum

subject: Dermatology
question: A 21-year-old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant present with worsening acne which she is finding distressing. She is currently using topical benzyl peroxide with limited effect. On examination there is widespread noninflammatory lesions and pustules on her face. What is the most appropriate next management step?
explanation:
Oral erythromycin may be used for acne in pregnancy. The other drugs are contraindicated Acne vulgaris: management Acne vulgaris is a common skin disorder which usually occurs in adolescence. It typically affects the face, neck and upper trunk and is characterised by the obstruction of the pilosebaceous follicles with keratin plugs which results in comedones, inflammation and pustules.

Acne may be classified into mild, moderate or severe: xmild: open and closed comedones with or without sparse inflammatory lesions xmoderate acne: widespread non-inflammatory lesions and numerous papules and pustules xsevere acne: extensive inflammatory lesions, which may include nodules, pitting, and scarring

A simple step-up management scheme often used in the treatment of acne is as follows: xsingle topical therapy (topical retinoids, benzyl peroxide) xtopical combination therapy (topical antibiotic, benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoid) xoral antibiotics: e.g. Oxytetracycline, doxycycline. Improvement may not be seen for 3-4 months. Minocycline is now considered less appropriate due to the possibility of irreversible pigmentation. Gram negative folliculitis may occur as a complication of long-term antibiotic use - high-dose oral trimethoprim is effective if this occurs xoral isotretinoin: only under specialist supervision

There is no role for dietary modification in patients with acne

question: Which one of the following factors would predispose a patient to forming keloid scars?

options.B: Incisions along relaxed skin tension lines

explanation:
Keloid scars - more common in young, black, male adults

Keloid scars Keloid scars are tumour-like lesions that arise from the connective tissue of a scar and extend beyond the dimensions of the original wound

Predisposing factors xethnicity: more common in people with dark skin xoccur more commonly in young adults, rare in the elderly xcommon sites (in order of decreasing frequency): sternum, shoulder, neck, face, extensor surface of limbs, trunk

Keloid scars are less likely if incisions are made along relaxed skin tension lines*

Treatment xearly keloids may be treated with intra-lesional steroids e.g. triamcinolone xexcision is sometimes required

*Langer lines were historically used to determine the optimal incision line. They were based on procedures done on cadavers but have been shown to produce worse cosmetic results than when following skin tension lines

question: A 65-year-old woman presents with bullae on her forearms following a recent holiday in Spain. She also notes that the skin on her hands is extremely fragile and tears easily. question: A 64-year-old woman presents with severe mucosal ulceration associated with the development of blistering lesions over her torso and arms. On examination the blisters are flaccid and easily ruptured when touched. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Blisters/bullae xno mucosal involvement: bullous pemphigoid xmucosal involvement: pemphigus vulgaris

Pemphigus vulgaris Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disease caused by antibodies directed against desmoglein, a cadherintype epithelial cell adhesion molecule. It is more common in the Ashkenazi Jewish population

Management xsteroids ximmunosuppressants

question: A 17-year-old man presents with a 2 week history of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and repeated episodes of flushing. Examination reveals urticarial skin lesions on the trunk. What test is most likely to reveal the diagnosis?
explanation:

question: A 54-year-old man presents with a two month history of a rapidly growing lesion on his right forearm. The lesion initially appeared as a red papule but in the last two weeks has become a crater filled centrally with yellow/brown material. On examination the man has skin type II, the lesion is 4 mm in diameter and is morphologically as described above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Keratoacanthoma Keratoacanthoma is a benign epithelial tumour. They are more frequent in middle age and do not become more common in old age (unlike basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma)

Features - said to look like a volcano or crater xinitially a smooth dome-shaped papule xrapidly grows to become a crater centrally-filled with keratin
